analysis.one_liner: Lets companies treat more workers as independent contractors outside minimum wage, overtime, and union protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in September 2023 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2025, with 9 Republican sponsors and no Democratic support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes a new, narrow definition of “employee” into two cornerstone labor laws: the Fair Labor Standards Act, which guarantees the federal minimum wage and overtime pay, and the National Labor Relations Act, which protects the right to unionize. Under the bill, a worker counts as an independent contractor — with none of those rights — unless the company controls the details of how the work is done and the worker bears entrepreneurial risks. It also bars companies' own requirements, like insurance, safety standards, and deadlines, from counting as evidence that someone is an employee. The bill was referred to committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that rely on contract labor — app-based ride-hailing and delivery platforms, staffing firms, franchisors, trucking and logistics operations — would gain, because a broader contractor classification frees them from paying minimum wage, overtime, or payroll taxes for those workers, and from bargaining obligations under labor law.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a two-part test under which a worker is an independent contractor unless the company exercises significant control over the details of how the work is performed and the worker bears entrepreneurial opportunities and risks, removing minimum wage, overtime, and collective bargaining rights from anyone who fails that test [S2].

It forbids counting a company's own requirements — legal compliance, stricter health and safety standards, mandatory insurance, and contractually agreed performance standards such as deadlines — as evidence that a worker is an employee, making it harder to establish employee status in practice [S2].

The same narrow standard is written into the National Labor Relations Act, so workers classified as contractors would also fall outside federal protections for union organizing and collective bargaining [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers shifted into contractor status would bear the cost: no guaranteed minimum wage or overtime pay, no employer payroll taxes funding Social Security and Medicare on their behalf, no unemployment insurance, and no federal right to unionize. Taxpayers and compliant employers also bear some cost, because workers without benefits often fall back on public assistance and honest employers face undercutting.

drawbacks.text: Workers reclassified as independent contractors would lose the federal minimum wage, overtime pay, and the legal right to organize and bargain collectively, since those protections apply exclusively to employees [S2].
The bill would make it harder to prove employment even when companies impose insurance mandates, safety standards, and deadlines, by barring those factors from the analysis entirely [S2].

A fair objection supporters raise: many workers genuinely prefer the flexibility of contracting, and existing classification tests are uncertain, so a clearer statutory line could reduce confusion — though this bill draws that line so broadly that whole categories of dependent workers would fall outside protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers companies lower labor costs and workers nominal flexibility, but the measurable trade is real: guaranteed wages, overtime, and bargaining rights in exchange for an uncertain entrepreneurial upside. Most workers classified under this standard would come out with fewer protections and no offsetting benefit, and compliant employers would face competition from those paying contractor rates.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Elise Stefanik introduced the bill on September 14, 2023, joined by Representatives Kevin Kiley and Michelle Steel as original sponsors [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce that same day, and the public record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
Eight Republican members cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The bill expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, workers kept their existing minimum wage, overtime, and union rights, and companies did not get the broader contractor exemption they sought.

for.name: Rep. Elise Stefanik
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write the new contractor standard into federal labor law

for.name: Reps. Kevin Kiley and Michelle Steel
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill on its first day

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill drew no Democratic support in a House where Republicans held 226 seats [S1, S4].

industries.industry: Gig economy platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, and app-based work)
industries.note: A broader contractor classification would let platforms treat drivers and couriers as contractors rather than employees, avoiding minimum wage, overtime, and collective bargaining obligations. Workers classified out of employee status bear the cost directly [S2].

industries.industry: Staffing, franchising, trucking, and logistics firms that rely on contract labor
industries.note: These businesses could reclassify dependent workers as contractors, cutting wage and payroll costs, and could not have their own insurance, safety, or deadline requirements counted against contractor status [S2].

Writing the narrow contractor test into the National Labor Relations Act would remove classified-out workers from federal collective bargaining protections, shrinking the pool of workers unions can organize [S3].
